title: Vincent Sunn Chen - The Art & Science of Benchmarking Agents

segments.text: VINCENT SUNN CHEN: Thank you so much for Berkeley and the RTI
group for putting together.
I'm Vincent.
I'm one of the founding team members and a research
leader at Snorkel.
We've spent years building data sets with Frontier Labs
and Enterprises and deploying these agents
in real-world scenarios.
And in this talk, I wanted to talk
about what makes benchmarks and evaluation
methods really effective and had actually make them last?
How do you build really robust measurement sticks that
are adopted by the field and actually influence
the way the field is going?
So really quickly about us.
We've been working on data for a very long time.
We have a number of academic groups,
from Chris Re's group at Stanford to Alex
and Fred's groups at Wisconsin and Washington.
And our key focus over the last decade plus
has really been on data-centric methods
for effective frontier AI.
And so we're really privileged these days
to be able to work with some of the best academic groups
out there in accelerating and partnering on some
of these open benchmarks.
We're very humbled to work with some of these awesome benchmarks
on the board.
Very own [INAUDIBLE], agents last exam.
We were very happy to help, as a data and research partner,
helping with some of the quality control mechanisms.
We've also partnered on a number of recent benchmarks,
including continual learning bench also
from Berkley out of the Skylab, OSWorld 2.0, and very recently,
the last few versions of terminal bench,
which actually just shipped in the last few weeks.
In this talk, I'm going to mention
some of the learnings we've had on our work on these benchmarks,
and maybe put out a little bit of a call for the types
of problems we think are going to be really important to solve
in this space here.
So the key problem here is that our ability to measure AI
has really been outpaced by our ability to develop it.
We're seeing that benchmarks in general
are becoming really, really important.
But they're also increasingly difficult to build.
There are new challenges when it comes to take coding.
Human eval, launched several years ago, was at 95%.
And most recently, the Harding program benchmarks are at 3%.
And as you climb the scale of complexity,
you find that it's increasingly challenging to actually
verify and evaluate a number of these tasks at the frontier.
Benchmarks have also never mattered more.
They are important for steering research agendas, model releases
and billions in computer actually pushed
towards a hill-climbing and addressing these benchmark gaps.
We think that building benchmarks
is a real research-focus area that is non-trivial.
Benchmaxxing is a real problem.
We think that models tuned to the test,
require a lot more thoughtful design and community
contribution to ensure that we're
providing really effective standards
and measuring sticks for the field.
What I call benchslop, the idea that you can really quickly
vibe code a benchmark and get a fancy Twitter post out
is increasingly a really large problem
where the individual task quality is lacking.
And a lot of effort needs to be put into designing
extremely high quality tasks.
And lastly, as model capabilities improve,
they also improve at reward hacking
and tricking and deceiving the benchmark builders,
where it becomes a bit of a cat and mouse game
in improving our methodology for building effective benchmarks.
So this is really hard.
And we want to talk a bit about some of our learnings
for addressing these challenges and some examples
that we've pursued.
The other angle I wanted to talk through here
was the fact that with agentic AI, the shape of data
is becoming increasingly non-trivial.
We move from a regime of much more simple prompt response
pairs or simple thumbs up, thumbs down
type of feedback mechanisms in terms of data labeling and data
development to a much more complex stack of data sets
in RL environments.
Right now, we're seeing entire environments or worlds built up
from rubrics to verifiers to tools with complex environments
that mimic our day-to-day settings.
And I'll note that this adds to the complexity in measuring
these types of data sets.
So as the surface area keeps expanding and certain tasks
continue saturating, you might think,
oh, we're done with certain fields.
Or we're done measuring coding, for instance.
And I challenge that as you push the frontier along a number
of axes of complexity here.
One of our views is that sequence length,
or the length of autonomy on the y-axis
is a really important axis.
And on the x-axis, we have input/output and environment
complexity.
Hey, what are the types of tasks or outputs that you're solving?
It becomes increasingly more important to drive
the next wave of benchmarks.
And so again, this is what I alluded to earlier.
There's a long tail and a very important space of problems
to measure in the coding space.
And despite coding becoming so impressive
in the last year or two years, we
think there's a lot of work to do in the benchmarking space
as well.
So I want to talk about one of the benchmarks
we recently pushed out and share a little bit of our philosophy,
interweaved, and how we built this
and what the principles are for building effective benchmarks.
We launched last month, something
called Senior SWE-Bench.
We were very fortunate to work with the original SWE-Bench team
over at Princeton.
And the key thesis for this benchmark
was the fact that our agents are moving
far beyond the level of junior engineering capabilities.
But we don't really have a good way
to evaluate them at the senior level.
What do you think of when you think of a senior engineer?
These are folks who can capture underspecified requirements.
They can take an ambiguous problem and run with it.
They have some notion of taste.
We tried to address all of these types of issues
in this next evolution of the SWE-Bench series.
So a few principles first.
We think that really effective benchmarks in general
are, one, important research agendas for the space.
And two, really well specified kind of measurement tools
in general.
And so, Senior SWE-Bench as I mentioned,
was the benchmark we're going to talk through here.
So number one, the research agenda.
We think that a lot of the greatest benchmarks
have a really strong thesis on the frontier.
They are making a bet on where the field is going.
I think the terminal bench team did a wonderful job
doing this right.
Several years ago, they made a bet
to say, hey, we think that the future of agents
is going to happen at the interface,
the text-based interface that agents and LLMs are already
doing a great job at.
I think that was very much a correct bet.
And we're seeing now that this is one of the most widely
adopted benchmarks on, I think, literally every frontier
model card.
We think the best benchmarks also
set a roadmap for the field.
Again, SWE-Bench released several years ago,
has now seen a big series that we
were very happy to contribute to the lineage of.
And the really great research tools
for setting the stage for our fellow colleagues to build on
top of.
And really, critically, we think the best benchmarks
consider researcher UX.
They really consider how do we make it easy for other folks
to build on top of this?
How do we build the right primitives
so that other members of the community
can actually contribute?
So how does this apply to Senior SWE-Bench?
What is our core thesis here?
A few different points I wanted to make.
Number one, we capture naturally under specified instructions.
So when you talk to a senior or principal engineer on Slack,
you're not specifying a full EDD.
You're not specifying line by line instructions
for what to do, what not to do, they're Slack messages.
They're, hey, here's a dump of error logs.
Go investigate this.
Or here's a few bullets on what I think the user stories are
going to look like.
Go figure this out.
So that was one of the key axes we
tried to capture working with our expert network,
but also a number of methods we built internally.
Two, we captured a much longer horizon of tasks.
So these are tasks that challenge engineering skills.
They capture multi-service changes.
They're not just a single patch in a very local way.
They intentionally target really complex, longer horizon tasks.
And three, we wanted to build this benchmark
as something that could scale in terms of something
that other researchers could build on top of.
It wasn't a one-time effort.
It was something that continually
sources from the latest and greatest open source
repos, and helps us measure a broader components of software
engineering viability.
And lastly, we wanted to capture this notion of taste.
This idea that taste and maintainability
is really important in modern high quality software
engineering.
And this was something that we saw
was actually lacking in the current wave of benchmarks.
So we introduced this notion of a tasteful solve.
this idea that not only are we measuring correctness,
but we're measuring notions of code base alignment, practice
alignment, bloat relative to an Oracle
PR, a number of different metrics
that you can look at on the actual blog post and website.
But capture notions of quality beyond simply correctness.
And so I'll shift now to the science.
What actually makes a benchmark a really strong measuring tool?
And a number of different-- this is
like a greatest hits tour of some of my favorite benchmarks.
And really quickly, task quality, really,
really critical.
GPQA was a benchmark several years
ago that I was really impressed by.
One of the appendix pages was one
of my favorite contributions, where they actually
talked about how the pain incentives and the mechanisms
of incentivizing contributors actually
led to really, really high quality distributional control.
Defining a concrete taxonomy, like an MMLU, which
was very ambitious of its time, and defining
an academic taxonomy.
Difficulty in headroom, making sure
that there's still room to run for these frontier models.
And a really robust methodology for how you actually source
and build tasks ends up being really, really important
for effective benchmarks.
And so I won't go into all the gory details here,
but we ended up implementing a very rigorous quality control
mechanism for this particular benchmark.
Every single task relied on a suite of both agentic, but also
expert in the loop.
Quality control methods to catch things
like non-determinism, false positive, and false negatives
in the verifiers.
And there were multiple experts, including myself and a bunch
of our senior researchers at Snorkel, who would painstakingly
look at every single task along with our expert networks,
real software engineers in the field,
to make sure that benchmarks like this
were really, really reliable at the end of the day.
So this is live.
This was actually just updated last week.
I promise you, we triple checked the results here.
But remarkably, there's a three way tie for first place
right now.
On the benchmark between Fable, Opus, and Sol,
which is actually quite remarkable
when you think about the Pareto efficiency curve.
Again, this is on the metric of tasteful solves.
So not only are these optimizing for correctness,
they're optimizing for code-based practice
and alignment to really senior engineering practices.
So check it out.
It's at senior-swe-bench.snorkel.ai.
Just wanted to quickly call out some
of our awesome collaborators.
This was led by our co-founder Henry at Snorkel,
along with the original SWE-Bench team,
Karthik's group, and Fred Sala, our chief scientist,
and some folks at Wisconsin.
And so the last thing I'll leave you with
is we think that the future of benchmarks
are going to need to capture a few really
key axes of differentiation.
Number one, we think we need to push the frontier of environment
complexity.
We need to push realism in terms of the types of workspaces
and worlds that we're all operating in on a day-to-day.
Not just simple prompts and responses,
but real code-based environments,
scientific computing environments, legal workflows
or real systems that people are working in on a day-to-day.
Number two, we need to push the autonomy horizon
for these models.
We need to push how far these models can actually
go when it comes to working autonomously and pulling humans
in a bunch of these settings as well.
And three, we want to push output complexity,
not just in verifiable fields, but nuanced fields
like legal and health care, where the definition of good
is actually not a very simple, closed-form solution like we've
seen with mathematics, for instance.
So I'll leave this with you.
And I guess final call to action is
we're funding a number of these benchmarks.
So if you're working on something exciting,
if you'd like to collaborate, check out benchmarks.snorkel.ai.
A number of benchmarks that we put up there
were in partnership with our open benchmarks grant.
And I'm really excited to continue pushing and measuring
the frontier with you all.
Thanks so much.
[APPLAUSE]
